name: Sikhism
line: Remember the One, earn an honest living and share what you have.

quote.text: Truth is high, but higher still is truthful living.
quote.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Sri Rag, page 62; a common English rendering

quotes.text: No one is my enemy and no one is a stranger. I get along with everyone.
quotes.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Kanara, page 1299; a common English rendering

quotes.text: Recognise the whole human race as one.
quotes.source: Manas ki jat sabhai ekai pahichanbo, from Akal Ustat in the Dasam Granth

quotes.text: From woman, man is born. So why call her bad, from whom kings are born?
quotes.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Asa di Var, page 473; abridged from a common English rendering

quotes.text: Through your will, may everyone prosper.
quotes.source: Tere bhane sarbat da bhala: the closing line of the Sikh congregational prayer

quotes.text: There is no Hindu and there is no Muslim.
quotes.source: His first words after his revelation at the river Bein, according to the Janamsakhi tradition

words.usage: From the Sanskrit for student. A Sikh is someone who is learning from the Guru.

words.meaning: Teacher; the one who brings light
words.usage: The ten human Gurus, then the scripture, and finally the divine Word itself.
The first words of the scripture and the best known Sikh symbol. One reality, of which everything is an expression.
The most common Sikh name for God, repeated in meditation.
The presence of the divine in everything. To remember it constantly is the heart of practice.
Keeping the Name in mind, by quiet repetition or simply by attention.
Work done for others with no thought of reward: cooking, cleaning shoes, serving food, building.
Every gurdwara feeds anyone who comes, free, every day. Everyone sits on the floor in rows and eats the same food.
The company of those who seek the truth. Sikh teaching holds that the Guru is present in it.
Sitting side by side to eat, with no order of rank. Emperors were asked to sit in it before meeting the Guru.
A Sikh place of worship. It is open to all, and its four doors face the four directions.
1,430 pages of hymns by six Gurus and by Hindu and Muslim saints, treated with the honour due to a sovereign.
The hymns of the scripture. They are set to ragas and meant to be sung.
The singing of gurbani with harmonium and tabla. The main form of Sikh worship.
The second pillar. Sikhs are to be householders who work, never beggars or recluses.
The third pillar: share your food and earnings before you consume them.
A tenth of one’s income given to the community and to those in need.
The will by which everything happens. To live in tune with it is the opposite of self-centredness.
The sense of separate self-importance. Guru Nanak calls it the deepest disease, and one that contains its own cure.
A person led by their own ego.
A person turned toward the truth and living by it.

words.meaning: The pure; those directly the Guru’s own
words.usage: The community of initiated Sikhs founded in 1699, committed to a discipline and to defending the weak.
Sweetened water stirred with a double-edged sword, used in the Khalsa initiation.
The last hours before dawn, held to be the best time for remembrance.
Steady, defiant optimism, kept up especially in hardship.
What Sikhs pray for at the end of every service: the good of everyone, everywhere.
The two swords of Guru Hargobind. A Sikh attends to both justice in the world and devotion.
A common Sikh greeting, and the answer to a victory call.
Warm pudding of flour, butter and sugar given to everyone at the end of a service. Receive it in cupped hands.
The tall saffron flag that marks every gurdwara, so a traveller can find food and shelter from far off.

practices.name: The ambrosial hour
practices.instructions: Rise before or near dawn and wash. Sit quietly with your back straight. Read aloud, or listen to, the opening of the Japji: there is one reality, truth is its name, the creator, without fear, without hatred, timeless, unborn, self-existent, known by grace. Then sit for ten minutes repeating a single word of remembrance on the breath. Use Waheguru if it sits well with you, or the word truth. When thoughts come, return.
practices.why: Guru Nanak’s Japji says: in the ambrosial hour before dawn, reflect on the true Name. Observant Sikhs begin every day this way, before the household wakes.
variations: Listen to the whole Japji Sahib, about twenty minutes.
Walk outside as it gets light, repeating the word in step.
If dawn is impossible, keep the first quarter-hour after waking.

practices.name: Honest work
practices.instructions: Before you start work, name the task and ask three questions. Is this work honest: does it cheat or mislead anyone? Am I giving a full measure for what I am paid? Whom does it serve? Then work hard and without complaint. During the day, when you catch yourself cutting a corner, put it right at once.
practices.why: Kirat karni, earning by one’s own honest labour, is one of the three pillars Guru Nanak taught. He himself farmed at Kartarpur in his last years. The tradition has no monks and no begging.
variations: Do one job today that is beneath your position.
Pay a debt or return something borrowed.
Thank someone whose labour you depend on.

practices.name: Share before you eat
practices.instructions: Before your main meal, share. Give part of your food to someone, pay for a stranger’s meal, or set aside a tenth of today’s earnings in a jar or an account kept for giving. Do it before you take your first mouthful. At the end of each week give away what has gathered.
practices.why: Vand chakna, sharing, is the third pillar. Sikhs set aside a tenth of income as dasvandh, and the free kitchen in every gurdwara is paid for and staffed by it.
variations: Eat with someone you would not usually sit with.
Take food to a shelter or a food bank.
Invite a neighbour to your table.

practices.name: Seva: serve with your hands
practices.instructions: Give twenty minutes to work that helps other people and earns you nothing: wash dishes that are not yours, sweep a shared place, carry, cook, serve, mend. Choose the humblest job available. Do not mention it. While you work, keep your word of remembrance going quietly.
practices.why: In gurdwaras people of every background cook, serve and clean side by side, and minding the shoes of the congregation is counted an honour. Service wears down haumai, the self-importance at the root of suffering.
variations: Volunteer at a gurdwara langar. Anyone may help.
Serve the people you live with, and eat last.
Pick up litter on your street.

practices.name: Evening song and the prayer for all
practices.instructions: At dusk sit down and listen to ten minutes of kirtan, the sung hymns of the Guru Granth Sahib, without doing anything else. Follow a translation if you can. Then stand, put your palms together and make a short prayer of your own in three parts: thanks for the day, mention of anyone who needs help, and last the wish that everyone, everywhere, may prosper.
practices.why: Sikhs recite Rehras at sunset and end every service standing for the Ardas, which closes with a prayer for the welfare of all humankind.
variations: Play the live broadcast from the Golden Temple.
End the day with Kirtan Sohila, the short bedtime prayer, in translation.

tasks.name: Eat a meal sitting on the floor beside someone, the same food for both
Visit a gurdwara, cover your head and eat in the langar
tasks.meta: Travel · all are welcome, every day

tasks.name: Listen to Asa di Var at dawn
Put a tenth of today’s income aside
Stand up for someone who is being treated unfairly
Journal: where did the self get in the way today?
Hukam: what are you fighting that simply is?
Greet a stranger as an equal and learn their name

rules.why: Give the first quarter-hour of the day to stillness and the Name, before news and messages.
No cheating, no padding, no living off others. Give a full day’s work.
Part of every meal and a tenth of every earning goes to someone else first.
Same greeting, same seat, same respect for the cleaner and the director. No one is a stranger.

rules.text: Serve with your hands every day
rules.why: One humble job for others, unpaid and unannounced.
No complaining today. Meet setbacks with chardi kala: rising spirits.

read.title: Hymns of the Sikh Gurus
read.creator: trans. Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh
read.why: A wide selection from the scripture in clear modern English, with the daily prayers complete.

read.title: Japji Sahib
read.creator: Guru Nanak; many translations
read.why: The morning prayer that opens the scripture. Thirty-eight stanzas on the One, the divine order and the stages of the journey.

read.title: Sikhism: A Very Short Introduction
read.creator: Eleanor Nesbitt
read.why: A reliable small book on history, practice and Sikh life today.

read.title: A History of the Sikhs
read.creator: Khushwant Singh
read.why: Two volumes by the great Punjabi man of letters. Readable and unsentimental.

read.title: The Sikhs
read.creator: Patwant Singh
read.why: One volume, told with feeling, from Nanak to 1984.

read.title: Train to Pakistan
read.creator: Khushwant Singh
read.why: A short novel of a border village in the summer of 1947, as Partition tears Sikh and Muslim neighbours apart.

watch.title: Himself He Cooks
watch.creator: Valérie Berteau and Philippe Witjes
watch.why: A wordless hour inside the kitchen of the Golden Temple, where volunteers feed tens of thousands every day.

watch.title: Chaar Sahibzaade
watch.creator: Harry Baweja
watch.why: An animated telling of the martyrdom of Guru Gobind Singh’s four sons. Loved by Sikh families.

watch.title: Punjab 1984
watch.creator: Anurag Singh
watch.why: A mother searches for her son during the insurgency years. A Punjabi film about how ordinary families lived through them.

watch.title: Bend It Like Beckham
watch.creator: Gurinder Chadha
watch.why: A British Punjabi Sikh girl wants to play football. Light, warm and exact about a diaspora household.

listen.title: Live kirtan from Sri Harmandir Sahib
listen.creator: Hazuri ragis of the Golden Temple
listen.why: Hymns are sung there from before dawn until late at night and broadcast live. Put it on and leave it on.

listen.title: Asa di Var
listen.creator: Bhai Surjan Singh, or the Golden Temple ragis
listen.why: Guru Nanak’s morning ballad, sung before sunrise. It contains the lines on the dignity of women.

listen.title: Japji Sahib
listen.creator: Recited by Bhai Tarlochan Singh and many others
listen.why: The morning prayer recited at an even pace. Twenty minutes.

listen.title: Gurbani in the original ragas
listen.creator: Bhai Avtar Singh and Bhai Gurcharan Singh
listen.why: Eleventh-generation musicians who kept the old melodic forms, with stringed instruments in place of the harmonium.

art.title: Sri Harmandir Sahib, the Golden Temple
art.creator: Amritsar, Punjab
art.year: founded 1577; gilded in the early 19th century
art.why: A low marble and gold shrine in the middle of a pool, reached by a causeway and entered by descending steps. Its four doors stand open to all sides.

art.title: Janamsakhi paintings
art.creator: Punjab workshops, such as the B-40 manuscript of 1733
art.why: Lively small pictures of the travels of Guru Nanak with Mardana the Muslim musician and Bala. The B-40 is in the British Library.

art.title: Portraits of Guru Nanak
art.creator: Sobha Singh
art.why: The gentle, white-bearded image with a raised hand that hangs in millions of Sikh homes. It is a modern devotional picture and no likeness survives.

art.title: Slough and EnTWINed
art.creator: The Singh Twins
art.why: Two British Sikh sisters paint diaspora life and imperial history in the jewelled style of Indian miniatures.

eat.title: Langar dal and roti
eat.creator: Black lentils simmered for hours, with flatbread
eat.why: The meal of every gurdwara: simple, vegetarian so that everyone can eat it, and served to all in the same rows.

eat.title: Karah prashad
eat.creator: Equal parts wholewheat flour, ghee and sugar, with water
eat.why: Stirred over heat while prayers are recited and given warm to everyone present.

eat.title: Sarson da saag and makki di roti
eat.creator: Mustard greens with maize flatbread and white butter
eat.why: The winter dish of Punjab’s farmers.

eat.title: Kheer
eat.creator: Rice pudding with cardamom
eat.why: Served in the langar on festival days.

drink.title: Lassi
drink.creator: Churned yogurt, salted or sweet
drink.why: The drink of Punjab, served in tall steel tumblers.

drink.title: Cha
drink.creator: Milky tea boiled with cardamom and fennel
drink.why: Tea is served to visitors in the langar hall at all hours.

drink.title: Sweet water at a chhabeel
drink.creator: Milk, water, sugar and rose syrup
drink.why: In the heat of June Sikhs set up roadside stalls and hand cold sweet drinks to every passer-by, in memory of Guru Arjan.

customs.title: Covering the head and removing shoes
customs.creator: On entering a gurdwara
customs.why: Everyone does both. Scarves are provided. Tobacco and alcohol are never brought in.

customs.title: Bowing to the Guru Granth Sahib
customs.creator: Matha tekna
customs.why: On entering the hall people walk to the scripture, kneel and touch the forehead to the floor. A visitor may simply stand respectfully, then sit on the floor with the congregation.

customs.title: The names Singh and Kaur
customs.creator: Lion and princess
customs.why: Given to all Khalsa Sikhs in 1699 to erase caste surnames and to give women a name of their own.

customs.title: The five Ks
customs.creator: Articles of the initiated
customs.why: Uncut hair, a wooden comb, a steel bracelet, cotton shorts and a short sword. They are articles of faith worn by initiated Sikhs, and visitors should not copy them.

games.title: Kabaddi
games.creator: Team sport · Punjab
games.why: A raider crosses the line on one breath, tags a defender and tries to get home. Punjab plays the circle style, and Sikh villages are its heartland.

games.title: Gatka
games.creator: Martial art · Punjab
games.why: The Sikh art of the stick and sword, practised to drums and displayed at festivals. Find a demonstration at Vaisakhi.

games.title: Field hockey
games.creator: Team sport
games.why: Punjab’s adopted game. Sikh players such as Balbir Singh Sr., who won three Olympic golds, made India the great hockey power of the mid twentieth century.

festivals.title: Vaisakhi
festivals.creator: 13 or 14 April
festivals.why: The spring harvest and the founding of the Khalsa in 1699. Processions, new flags on every gurdwara and street langars.

festivals.title: Guru Nanak Gurpurab
festivals.creator: November, at the full moon of Kartik
festivals.why: The founder’s birthday. The whole scripture is read aloud without a break over forty-eight hours beforehand.

festivals.title: Bandi Chhor Divas
festivals.creator: October or November, on Diwali
festivals.why: The day of release, when Guru Hargobind left prison bringing fifty-two captive princes with him. The Golden Temple is lit with lamps.

festivals.title: Hola Mohalla
festivals.creator: March, the day after Holi
festivals.why: Three days of mock battles, riding and poetry at Anandpur Sahib, begun by Guru Gobind Singh.

places.title: Sri Harmandir Sahib
places.creator: Amritsar, Punjab, India
places.why: The Golden Temple. Walk the marble path round the pool, listen, and eat in the langar, which serves around a hundred thousand meals a day. Go before dawn as well.

places.title: Anandpur Sahib
places.creator: Punjab, India
places.why: The town where the Khalsa was created. The Virasat-e-Khalsa museum here tells Sikh history in a building by Moshe Safdie.

places.title: Gurdwara Darbar Sahib, Kartarpur
places.creator: Narowal, Pakistan
places.why: Where Guru Nanak farmed and died. Since 2019 a visa-free corridor has let pilgrims cross from India for the day. Check that it is open.

places.title: Gurdwara Bangla Sahib
places.creator: New Delhi, India
places.why: A gold-domed gurdwara with a large pool in the middle of the capital. An easy and welcoming first visit.

places.title: Gurdwara Sri Guru Singh Sabha
places.creator: Southall, London, United Kingdom
places.why: One of the largest gurdwaras outside India. The langar is open every day.

ethics.title: Equality
ethics.text: The Gurus rejected caste, taught the equal dignity of women and men and built the free kitchen so that everyone would eat together. There is one light in all.
ethics.practice: Share a meal or a table today with someone of a different standing from your own.

ethics.title: Honest labour
ethics.text: Guru Nanak chose to eat the coarse bread of a carpenter over a rich official’s feast, saying that honest bread holds milk and extorted bread holds blood.
ethics.practice: Look at where your money came from this month. Is any of it not clean?

ethics.title: Service
ethics.text: Seva is done with body, mind and wealth. It is owed to everyone without distinction, as when Bhai Kanhaiya gave water to wounded enemies on the battlefield.
ethics.practice: Help someone today who is not on your side.

ethics.title: Courage for justice
ethics.text: A Sikh is to be a saint-soldier: gentle, and ready to defend the oppressed. Guru Tegh Bahadur gave his life for the right of another religion to exist.
ethics.practice: Speak up once today where staying quiet would be easier.

ethics.title: Contentment
ethics.text: Santokh is being at ease with what one has while working hard. It guards against the five thieves: lust, anger, greed, attachment and pride.
ethics.practice: Name which of the five thieves visited you today.

ethics.title: Humility
ethics.text: The scripture is fanned and carried on the head, and its Gurus described themselves as the lowest of the low. Greatness is measured by service.
ethics.practice: Let someone else take the credit today.

philosophy.title: One
philosophy.text: The scripture begins with the numeral one. There is a single reality, without form or gender, present in everything and beyond everything. All religions’ names for it are accepted.
philosophy.practice: Look for the same light in three people you meet today.

philosophy.title: The Name
philosophy.text: Naam is the divine as it sounds through the world. Remembering it, by repetition and by attention, slowly re-tunes a person from self-centred to centred on the One.
philosophy.practice: Set three alarms today. At each, stop for one minute and remember.

philosophy.title: The disease of I
philosophy.text: Haumai, the sense of I and mine, is what separates a person from others and from God. It cannot be removed by ritual or by willpower. It dissolves through remembrance, service and grace.
philosophy.practice: Count how many of your sentences today begin with I.

philosophy.title: The divine order
philosophy.text: Everything happens within hukam. To recognise it is to stop saying I did this, and to act fully while accepting what comes. Guru Nanak says the one who understands it has no ego.
philosophy.practice: Take one thing you are resisting and act as if it had been given to you on purpose.

philosophy.title: Householder, not hermit
philosophy.text: The Gurus married, worked and raised children. Liberation is found, in the scripture’s image, like the lotus that lives in water and stays dry.
philosophy.practice: Find the sacred in one domestic chore today.

philosophy.title: The three pillars
philosophy.text: Remember the Name, earn honestly, share with others. They are meant to be done together: devotion without work is idle, work without sharing is greed.
philosophy.practice: Check which pillar is shortest in your life this week.

philosophy.title: Saint and soldier
philosophy.text: Guru Hargobind wore two swords, for spiritual and worldly authority. Prayer and justice belong together, and force is allowed only as a last resort in defence of the weak.
philosophy.practice: Ask what you would defend, and what it would cost you.

philosophy.title: The Word as Guru
philosophy.text: In 1708 the last human Guru named the scripture as his successor. Authority passed from a person to a text sung in community, so that no one could own it.
philosophy.practice: Read one hymn slowly aloud and ask what it asks of you today.

What did you remember in the first hour?

When were you a learner today?
What did the music do?
Whose labour fed you?
What do you want credit for?
Where did you stay silent when you should have spoken?
What does the welfare of all require of you?

What did serving with your hands teach you about yourself?

Which pillar will you keep building?

intro: Sikhism began in Punjab at the end of the fifteenth century with a man named Nanak. He was born in 1469 to a Hindu family in a village west of Lahore, in a region ruled by Muslims. Around the age of thirty he disappeared while bathing in a river and returned three days later saying: there is no Hindu, there is no Muslim. He spent the next two decades travelling, by tradition as far as Mecca, Tibet and Sri Lanka, with a Muslim musician named Mardana, singing what he had understood.

What he taught was simple and hard. There is one God, formless and present in everyone. No ritual, pilgrimage, caste or priest brings a person closer. What does is to remember the divine Name, to earn a living by honest work and to share what one earns. Women and men, high and low, are equal. He settled at last as a farmer at Kartarpur, where his followers, called Sikhs or learners, worked, sang and ate together.

Nine Gurus followed him, and each added to the community. The free kitchen was made a fixed rule. The city of Amritsar was founded and its temple built with doors on four sides. The fifth Guru, Arjan, compiled the hymns of his predecessors and of Hindu and Muslim saints into a scripture, and was tortured to death by the Mughal emperor in 1606. After that the Gurus bore arms. The ninth, Tegh Bahadur, was beheaded in Delhi in 1675 for defending the freedom of Hindus to practise their religion.

His son, Guru Gobind Singh, gave the community its final form. On the spring festival of 1699 he founded the Khalsa, an order of initiated women and men committed to a strict discipline, to equality and to the defence of the weak, marked by five articles of faith including uncut hair. Before his death in 1708 he declared that there would be no more human Gurus. The scripture, the Guru Granth Sahib, is the Guru, and it is treated as a living sovereign.

There are about twenty-five million Sikhs today, most in Indian Punjab, with large communities in Britain, Canada, the United States, East Africa and Australia. Wherever they have settled there is a gurdwara, and in every gurdwara there is a kitchen that feeds anyone who walks in, free, with no questions.

This Onda follows the three pillars through a day: remembrance before dawn, honest work, sharing before eating, service with the hands and song at dusk. You are a guest. The articles of faith and the initiation belong to committed Sikhs, and you are not asked to adopt them. A visit to a gurdwara, though, is open to everyone, and you will be fed.
guide.origin: Punjab, the land of five rivers, now divided between India and Pakistan
guide.era: Guru Nanak was born in 1469. The line of ten Gurus ended in 1708 with the scripture as Guru

figures.name: Guru Nanak
figures.bio: The founder. Poet, traveller and farmer. His 974 hymns are the foundation of the scripture.

figures.name: Bhai Mardana
figures.bio: A Muslim musician of the minstrel caste who accompanied Nanak on the rabab for decades. The first Sikh after the Guru’s sister.

figures.name: Guru Amar Das
figures.bio: The third Guru. He made eating in the langar a condition of meeting him, appointed women as preachers and opposed the veil and widow burning.

figures.name: Guru Arjan
figures.bio: The fifth Guru. He completed the Harmandir Sahib, compiled the scripture in 1604 and became the first Sikh martyr.

figures.name: Guru Hargobind
figures.bio: The sixth Guru, who wore two swords, built the Akal Takht as a seat of worldly authority and trained the Sikhs to defend themselves.

figures.name: Guru Tegh Bahadur
figures.bio: The ninth Guru. Executed in Delhi after he took up the cause of Kashmiri Hindus who faced forced conversion.

figures.name: Guru Gobind Singh
figures.bio: The tenth Guru: poet, warrior and founder of the Khalsa. He lost his father, his mother and all four sons to the struggle.

figures.name: Mai Bhago
figures.bio: A woman who shamed forty deserters into returning and led them into battle at Muktsar in 1705. She later served as one of the Guru’s bodyguards.

figures.name: Maharaja Ranjit Singh
figures.bio: The one-eyed ruler who united Punjab into a Sikh kingdom, employed ministers of every faith and gave the gold for the temple at Amritsar.

figures.name: Bhagat Puran Singh
figures.bio: He carried a disabled boy on his back for years and founded Pingalwara in Amritsar, a home for the destitute and sick that still runs on donations.

history.detail: At Talwandi, now Nankana Sahib in Pakistan. He works as a storekeeper for a local governor before his calling.
Nanak vanishes into the Bein and emerges with his message. He gives away his goods and begins his travels.
He founds a village on the Ravi, farms, and establishes the pattern of work, worship and shared meals.
Guru Ram Das digs the pool of nectar. His son Arjan builds the Harmandir in its centre, lower than the surrounding ground and open on four sides.
The Adi Granth, written out by Bhai Gurdas, is placed in the Harmandir. It includes hymns by Kabir, Farid, Ravidas and other saints of both religions and all castes.
He is tortured to death at Lahore on the orders of the emperor Jahangir. His son takes up arms.
He is beheaded in Chandni Chowk, Delhi, under Aurangzeb. Gurdwara Sis Ganj stands on the site.
At Anandpur on Vaisakhi day, Gobind Singh calls for a volunteer to give his head. Five come forward, are initiated with sweetened water and then initiate him.
Dying of stab wounds at Nanded, Guru Gobind Singh ends the human line and vests authority in the scripture and the community.
Ranjit Singh takes Lahore and rules an empire from the Khyber to the Sutlej. Ten years after his death it falls to the British after two wars.
British troops kill hundreds at a Vaisakhi gathering in Jallianwala Bagh. Soon after, a non-violent campaign wins control of the gurdwaras for an elected Sikh body.
Punjab is cut in two. Millions of Sikhs leave their homes and holy places in the west, and hundreds of thousands of people of all communities die.

history.what: The assault on the Golden Temple and after
history.detail: In June the Indian army storms the temple complex to remove armed militants, with heavy loss of life. After two Sikh bodyguards assassinate the prime minister in October, mobs kill thousands of Sikhs in Delhi and elsewhere.

concepts.detail: God is single, formless, without fear or enmity, beyond birth and death, and known through grace. The opening statement, the Mul Mantar, is recited daily.
Both the name of God and God’s presence pervading creation. Naam japna, remembering the Name, is the first pillar.
The root problem: living as though one were separate and central. Its five outgrowths are lust, anger, greed, attachment and pride.
The will or command by which the universe runs. Wisdom is to recognise it and act in harmony with it.
Effort is required, but liberation finally comes as a gift. This keeps the devout from pride in their own virtue.
Sikhs hold that a single guiding light passed through ten human teachers and now rests in the scripture and in the gathered community.
Worshipping together and eating together as equals. The two institutions that made a community out of followers.
Initiated Sikhs keep the five articles of faith, rise early to pray, give a tenth and abstain from tobacco, intoxicants and adultery.
The principle that religion must concern itself with justice in the world. The Akal Takht faces the Harmandir Sahib for this reason.

facts.text: The kitchen of the Golden Temple serves between fifty thousand and a hundred thousand free meals every day, almost entirely with volunteer labour.
The Guru Granth Sahib has 1,430 pages in every printed copy, with the same hymn on the same page everywhere.
The scripture is arranged by musical mode: thirty-one ragas, with instructions on how each hymn is to be sung.
Each night the scripture is carried in procession to a bedchamber and each morning it is brought back and opened at random for the order of the day.
The steel bracelet has no beginning and no end, and it is on the hand that works.
Sikhs are about two per cent of India’s population and have long made up a far larger share of its army.

sensitivity.note: Sikhism is a living faith with a strong sense of identity. This Onda borrows the three pillars and the spirit of service. It does not ask you to wear the articles of faith or to imitate initiation, and it is no substitute for the sangat, the Sikh congregation.
requiredCaveats: The turban and the five Ks are articles of faith. They are not costume.
The Guru Granth Sahib is treated as a living Guru. Printed or digital gurbani should be handled with respect.
The events of 1984 and of Partition are within living memory and remain painful.
Sikhs are often mistaken for members of other religions and have suffered violence because of it. Learn the difference.
